extracted.intended_audience: patent practitioners, patent examiners, claim drafters, patent agents
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance on the meaning and effect of transitional phrases in patent claims (e.g., 'comprising', 'consisting of', 'consisting essentially of', 'having', 'composed of') and how those phrases determine whether additional unrecited elements or steps are excluded from claim scope.

rubrics_metrics.name: "comprising" (open-ended/inclusive)
rubrics_metrics.description: "The transitional term 'comprising', which is synonymous with 'including,' 'containing,' or 'characterized by,' is inclusive or open-ended and does not exclude additional, unrecited elements or method steps."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use of 'comprising' signals that the named elements are essential but other elements may be added and still fall within the claim scope. Case law: Mars Inc. v. H.J. Heinz Co.; Invitrogen Corp. v. Biocrest Mfg.; Genentech, Inc. v. Chiron Corp.; Moleculon Research Corp. v. CBS, Inc.; In re Baxter; Ex parte Davis. Example: In Gillette Co. v. Energizer Holdings, the use of 'comprising' in the preamble and 'group of' made the claim presumptively open-ended, covering razors with more than three blades. Interpret 'comprising' as leaving the claim open for inclusion of unspecified ingredients or steps even in major amounts.

rubrics_metrics.name: "consisting of" (closed/exclusive)
rubrics_metrics.description: "The transitional phrase 'consisting of' excludes any element, step, or ingredient not specified in the claim."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat 'consisting of' as closed language that generally prevents inclusion of unrecited elements. Case law: In re Gray; Ex parte Davis (defines 'consisting of' as closing the claim to inclusion of other materials except ordinary impurities). Note exceptions/facts matter: Norian Corp. v. Stryker Corp. — a kit 'consisting of' claimed chemicals was found to be infringed even though it included an unrelated spatula because the spatula was unrelated to the claimed invention. Also, a claim depending from a 'consists of' claim generally cannot add an element or step. When 'consists of' appears in a clause of the body (not immediately after the preamble), it limits only that clause's element set; it does not necessarily close the claim as a whole (Mannesmann Demag Corp. v. Engineered Metal Products Co.; In re Crish example). 'Group consisting of' is often used to signal a closed Markush-type group.

rubrics_metrics.name: "consisting essentially of" (middle ground / material-effect test)
rubrics_metrics.description: "The transitional phrase 'consisting essentially of' limits the scope of a claim to the specified materials or steps 'and those that do not materially affect the basic and novel characteristic(s)' of the claimed invention."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: 'Consisting essentially of' is intermediate between fully open 'comprising' and fully closed 'consisting of.' Key points: (1) Determine what the basic and novel characteristics are (read the specification); absent a clear indication of those characteristics, courts may construe 'consisting essentially of' as equivalent to 'comprising' for prior art purposes (PPG Industries v. Guardian Industries). (2) Applicant bears the burden of showing that introduction of additional steps/components would materially change the invention (In re De Lajarte; Ex parte Hoffman). (3) Specification can define quantitative or qualitative limits that establish what would be a material change (AK Steel Corp. v. Sollac — silicon >0.5% materially altered properties). (4) Although typically used for compositions, it can be applied to method steps if read in light of the specification (Ex parte Hoffman). Case law: In re Herz; PPG Industries; Atlas Powder; In re Janakirama-Rao; Water Technologies Corp. v. Calco; AK Steel; In re De Lajarte; Ex parte Hoffman.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clause-level vs preamble-level use of transitional terms
rubrics_metrics.description: When transitional language such as 'consists of' appears in a clause of the body of a claim rather than immediately following the preamble, it limits only the element set forth in that clause; other elements are not necessarily excluded from the claim as a whole.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Read transitional language in context. Example: Mannesmann Demag Corp. v. Engineered Metal Products Co. and In re Crish — use of 'consists' in a clause did not limit the entire claim due to the presence of 'comprising' elsewhere; 'comprising' can preserve openness for other portions of the claim. In claim construction, determine which portion of the claim the transitional phrase attaches to and apply limits accordingly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interpretation of other transitional phrases ('having', 'composed of', etc.)
rubrics_metrics.description: Transitional phrases such as 'having' and 'composed of' must be interpreted in light of the specification to determine whether open or closed claim language is intended; 'composed of' has been interpreted as either 'consisting of' or 'consisting essentially of' depending on facts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not assume a single default for terms like 'having' or 'composed of.' Case law: Lampi Corp. v. American Power Products (term 'having' interpreted as open); Crystal Semiconductor Corp. v. TriTech Microelectronics (no presumption that 'having' opens the claim); Regents of the Univ. of Cal. v. Eli Lilly (term 'having' permitted inclusion of other moieties). 'Composed of' may be treated like 'consisting of' or 'consisting essentially of' depending on specification and evidence (AFG Industries v. Cardinal IG; In re Bertsch). Always interpret such transitional language in light of the specification and relevant facts.
